scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that new leadership can revitalise an enterprise while arguing a rigid rule loses experience; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: New energy can breathe life into an organisation that has grown tired.
One claim holds that those in power should step down after five years, on the reason that new leadership is the surest path to revitalising any enterprise.
I agree that fresh leadership often helps, but I believe a strict five-year rule and its reason both go too far.

sections.role: Body 1 — How new leadership can revitalise

sentences.text: First, there is real truth in the reason that new leadership can revitalise an enterprise.
A new leader often brings fresh ideas, new energy, and a willingness to change.
For example, a struggling company can be transformed when a bold new leader takes charge.
This shows that a change at the top can break old habits and renew an organisation.
Leaders who stay too long may grow stale, complacent, or resistant to any change.
Regular renewal can keep an enterprise lively and open to new possibilities.
To this extent, the reason behind the claim holds genuine value.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why a rigid rule loses experience

sentences.text: Second, however, forcing everyone out after five years would also do real harm.
New leadership is not always better, and constant change can bring instability.
Consider a skilled leader removed by the rule just as her long plans were starting to succeed.
Such a loss shows that experience and continuity also matter for an enterprise's success.
A fixed limit ignores that some leaders keep improving and renewing things for many years.
Revitalisation can also come from new ideas within an organisation, not only from new leaders.
Fresh leadership, then, is valuable but should not be forced on a rigid timetable.
In conclusion, new leadership can genuinely revitalise a tired enterprise.
But a strict five-year rule would waste experience and cause needless instability.
The wisest organisations welcome renewal without forcing out every leader at a fixed moment.
